paragraphs.heading: The study of layers
paragraphs.text: Stratigraphy is the branch of geology that studies rock layers, called strata, and the way rock is layered. It is mostly used on sedimentary rocks and on volcanic rocks that form in layers. It has three related subfields: lithostratigraphy, based on rock type; biostratigraphy, based on fossils; and chronostratigraphy, based on age.

paragraphs.heading: Steno, Arduino and Smith
paragraphs.text: Nicholas Steno, a Catholic priest, laid the theoretical basis in a 1669 work, where he set out three ideas: the law of superposition, plus the principles of original horizontality and of lateral continuity. In 1759 the Italian geologist Giovanni Arduino divided Earth's crust into four successive orders, Primary, Secondary, Tertiary and Quaternary, which is seen as the starting point of modern stratigraphy. William Smith, known as the "Father of English geology", made the first practical large-scale use of it from the 1790s. He saw how fossil markers could match up strata, and he created the first geological map of England.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the layers
paragraphs.text: The visible layering in rock comes from physical differences in rock type, which geologists call lithology. These changes can run up and down, as layers known as bedding, or sideways, and they reflect changes in the setting where the sediment was laid down, known as facies change. The most basic idea in the field is the law of superposition: in a sequence that has not been deformed, the oldest strata sit at the base.

paragraphs.heading: Fossils as time markers
paragraphs.text: Biostratigraphy rests on the fossils found in rock layers. Strata in widely separated places that hold the same fossil animals and plants can be treated as matching in time. It grew out of William Smith's principle of faunal succession, which came before the theory of biological evolution and became one of the first and strongest lines of evidence for it. The geologic time scale was built on this evidence during the 19th century, and it stayed a relative scale until radiometric dating supplied absolute dates, which led to chronostratigraphy.

paragraphs.heading: Gaps in the record
paragraphs.text: A gap where layers are missing from an area's record is called a stratigraphic hiatus. It can come from a pause in the laying down of sediment. Or the layers may have been removed by erosion, in which case the gap may be called a stratigraphic vacuity. A geologic fault can also make a hiatus appear.

paragraphs.heading: Magnetic signals in rock
paragraphs.text: Magnetostratigraphy is a way of dating sedimentary and volcanic sequences. As very fine magnetic grains sink through water, they act like tiny compasses and line up with Earth's magnetic field, and that direction is kept once they are buried. In lava, magnetic minerals line up with the field and are fixed when the lava crystallizes. Layers formed when the field pointed as it does today show normal polarity, while those formed when the North Magnetic Pole lay near the South Rotational Pole show reversed polarity. The pattern from a site is then compared with the Global Magnetic Polarity Time Scale.
